Definition: Whether authentication is possible through a centralized government portal or digital gateway
Comments: No operational centralized government portal with national ID authentication exists. The DPI Map records 'Enables authentication via government portal: NA'. Libya has limited e-government infrastructure. The General Information Authority's LY-GOVREP platform (launched July 2025) is an internal government reporting tool, not a citizen-facing portal using ID authentication. No documented national citizen e-services portal with ID-based login has been found.

revised_comments: Libya operates 'Dawlaty', a national e-government portal run by the state-owned Libya Telecom and Technology Holding Company (LPTIC), alongside the longer-standing e-Portal supervised by the General Information Authority (GIA). Neither currently authenticates users via the national digital identity system: login to Dawlaty relies on basic username and password credentials rather than verified digital ID. GIA is piloting the second level of its National Digital Identity System (LY-DNID), intended to extend citizen-facing identity verification and multi-level authentication integrated with the National Data Distributor (LY-NDEX), but as of the most recent update this remains in technical trials with banking partners and has not yet been launched as a citizen-facing authentication channel through the government portal.

Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: No evidence of a citizen self-service portal or mechanism enabling individuals to access their personal data held in the national identity database. The DPI Map records 'Identity act clarifies relationship with feeder documents: NA'. Law No. 6 of 2022, Article 77, grants the right to access and update personal data held by electronic authentication service providers, but no operational citizen data access portal for national ID records has been documented. Libya's digital government services remain very limited.

revised_comments: Libya's Electronic Transactions Law (Law No. 6 of 2022), Article 77, grants individuals the right to access and update personal data held by accredited electronic authentication service providers, and requires that appropriate technological means be provided to enable electronic access. This provision applies to certificate-issuing authentication providers under the e-transactions regime rather than explicitly to the National ID Number database held by the Civil Registry Authority under Law No. 8 of 2014. No self-service portal, mobile application, or documented formal request procedure allowing citizens to view their national ID record or an access log has been identified.

Together these instruments constitute a specific legal framework addressing digital identity and electronic authentication, distinct from the general National ID Number legislation of Law No. 8 of 2014.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: No data protection authority exists in Libya. The DPI Map records 'National Data Protection Act exists: NO' and no dedicated DPA has been established. The National Information Security and Safety Authority (NISSA), established by Decree No. 28 of 2013, oversees cybersecurity and electronic authentication but is not a data protection authority. Its policies are binding only on the public sector. No independent authority with mandate to oversee personal data processing, receive complaints, or enforce data protection rules has been created.

revised_comments: Libya has no dedicated data protection authority. Both the DLA Piper Data Protection Laws of the World guide and OneTrust DataGuidance confirm the absence of a general data protection authority in Libya. The National Information Security and Safety Authority (NISSA), established by Decree No. 28 of 2013, oversees cybersecurity and accredits electronic authentication service providers, but its personal-data-protection policies bind only public-sector bodies, and it does not function as an independent regulator with a mandate to receive complaints or enforce data protection rules across the identity system.

Comments: No credible evidence found on whether the Libyan national ID card is free or charged to citizens. No official government pricing documentation for the national ID card has been located in public sources. The NIN issuance from birth is an administrative process tied to civil registration, but whether the physical card carries a fee is undocumented in available sources.

revised_comments: The Libyan national identity card is not issued free of charge. The US Department of State's visa reciprocity and civil documents schedule for Libya records a fee of 3.5 Libyan Dinars for the identity card ('Bitaket Shakhsiah'). Earlier legislation (Law No. 18 of 1963 on personal ID cards) similarly permitted the Minister to impose a card fee, historically capped at 250 Libyan pounds. Registration for the underlying National ID Number itself, tied to civil registration, appears to be administratively free, but issuance of the physical credential attracts a nominal fee.

Definition: Whether ID system undergoes regular security audits, penetration testing, or vulnerability assessments
Comments: No publicly documented regular security audits or independent third-party assessments of Libya's national identity system were found. The DPI Map records 'Data leak disclosure process exists: NO'. Libya's House of Representatives Defence and National Security Committee warned in December 2025 of 'manipulation and serious violations' within the Civil Registry Authority allowing foreign nationals to unlawfully obtain Libyan NINs — indicating systemic security failures without evidence of formal security reviews. NISSA (established 2013) oversees ICT security but no published security audit of the identity system exists. Libya scores partially on the NCSI cybersecurity index (60% on strategic indicators) but no ID-specific security review is documented.
